views.name: clean_runner_orders_numeric
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  order_id,
  runner_id,
  pickup_time,
  distance AS distance,
  duration AS duration,
  cancellation
FROM pizza_clean_runner_orders
UNION ALL
SELECT
  order_id,
  runner_id,
  pickup_time,
  CAST(NULLIF(REPLACE(REPLACE(distance,'km',''), ' ', ''), '') AS REAL) AS distance,
  -- remove REGEXP_REPLACE; strip non-numeric chars by chaining common replacements and fallback to NULL if empty
  CAST(NULLIF(REPLACE(REPLACE(REPLACE(duration, 'h', '.'), 'm', ''), ' ', ''), '') AS REAL) AS duration,
  cancellation
FROM pizza_runner_orders
WHERE distance IS NOT NULL OR duration IS NOT NULL

semantic_filters.cancellation: IS NULL OR cancellation IS NOT NULL

params.description: Normalized per-runner-per-order numeric metrics (distance, duration) and pickup time for orders handled by runners, suitable for analytics or further aggregation.
params.when_to_use: Calculate per-order or per-runner aggregates (counts, sums, averages) of distance or duration. | Filter or segment orders by runner, pickup_time, distance, duration, or cancellation status before joining to other datasets. | Serve as the numeric foundation when composing higher-level metrics (e.g., average delivery distance per runner, median duration per day) without re-parsing raw text fields.
params.output_schema: order_id: unique identifier of the order at the grain of this view; derived from pizza_clean_runner_orders.order_id and pizza_runner_orders.order_id | runner_id: identifier of the runner assigned to the order; derived from pizza_clean_runner_orders.runner_id and pizza_runner_orders.runner_id | pickup_time: timestamp (or datetime) when the runner picked up the order; derived from pizza_clean_runner_orders.pickup_time and pizza_runner_orders.pickup_time | distance: numeric (REAL) distance for the run (normalized). From pizza_clean_runner_orders.distance (already numeric) or parsed CAST(...) AS REAL of pizza_runner_orders.distance after stripping 'km' and spaces. NULL if not present/parsable. | duration: numeric (REAL) duration for the run (normalized). From pizza_clean_runner_orders.duration or parsed CAST(...) AS REAL of pizza_runner_orders.duration after simple character replacements. NULL if not present/parsable. | cancellation: cancellation indicator/status for the order-runner row. From pizza_clean_runner_orders.cancellation and pizza_runner_orders.cancellation
params.grounded_columns: pizza_clean_runner_orders.order_id | pizza_clean_runner_orders.runner_id | pizza_clean_runner_orders.pickup_time | pizza_clean_runner_orders.distance | pizza_clean_runner_orders.duration | pizza_clean_runner_orders.cancellation | pizza_runner_orders.order_id | pizza_runner_orders.runner_id | pizza_runner_orders.pickup_time | pizza_runner_orders.distance | pizza_runner_orders.duration | pizza_runner_orders.cancellation
params.metric: distance = distance (numeric) — value taken directly from pizza_clean_runner_orders.distance when present; otherwise CAST(NULLIF(REPLACE(REPLACE(distance,'km',''), ' ', ''), '') AS REAL) applied to pizza_runner_orders.distance, producing a REAL or NULL | duration = duration (numeric) — value taken directly from pizza_clean_runner_orders.duration when present; otherwise CAST(NULLIF(REPLACE(REPLACE(REPLACE(duration, 'h', '.'), 'm', ''), ' ', ''), '') AS REAL) applied to pizza_runner_orders.duration, producing a REAL or NULL | cancellation = cancellation (as provided) — passthrough from source tables | row_grain = (order_id, runner_id) — the view guarantees one row per order_id/runner_id occurrence present in the unioned sources
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to orders_with_runner_metrics on (order_id, runner_id) — safe because orders_with_runner_metrics is expected to be at the same or a coarser grain (one row per order-runner metrics or per order) so this view's rows will match one-to-one or many-to-one without duplicating the numeric measures. If the target is one-to-one, sums/averages on distance/duration remain correct. | join to orders_with_pizza_and_customer_clean on order_id — safe when orders_with_pizza_and_customer_clean is one-row-per-order (not one-to-many for items). This will attach order-level customer/pizza attributes without duplicating the runner measures. | join to companies_with_industry_and_dates or company_funding_summary_by_company on company identifier (if a company dimension is present via runner or order) — safe only if the company side is one-row-per-company. Joining a one-row-per-company table will not multiply measures. | do NOT join directly to pizza_recipe_topping_expansion, pizza_toppings_with_names, or any reshaped orders-to-toppings table without first aggregating those tables up to order_id (or order_id, runner_id) — those are one-to-many (an order has multiple toppings). Directly joining them will multiply rows and thus multiply distance/duration measures. Instead: pre-aggregate toppings to order_id (e.g., COUNT, ARRAY_AGG) before joining. | do NOT join directly to trees_by_ntaname, income_by_zipcode, or latest_statistics_per_state unless you join on a true one-to-one key (e.g., zipcode -> income_by_zipcode where income is one-row-per-zipcode). If the geographic/statistics table is one-row-per-geography, joining on the matching geography key is safe; if that table is many-to-many or contains multiple time-stamped rows per geography, aggregate or filter it to one row per geography first. | when composing further aggregations over this view (e.g., SUM(distance) or AVG(duration) by runner_id or date(pickup_time)), you can aggregate directly because the view is already at the atomic measure grain (order_id, runner_id). Avoid aggregating after joining to one-to-many dimensions unless those dimensions were reduced to one row per order_id/runner_id. | in short: safe to join to true dimensions keyed one-to-one with order_id or runner_id; unsafe to join to any table that is one-to-many on order_id (toppings, items, events) without re-aggregation to order-level to prevent measure multiplication.

views.description: Normalized runner order events with numeric distance and duration. Use when queries need consistent numeric measures for distance/duration and to prefer cleaned numeric source but fall back to parsing textual fields when only text exists. | Use for: Compare average/median runner distance or duration; Identify slow deliveries or outlier durations; Join runner performance to orders/customers

views.name: orders_with_pizza_and_customer_clean
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  pcco.order_id,
  pcco.customer_id,
  pcco.pizza_id,
  pn.pizza_name,
  pcco.exclusions,
  pcco.extras,
  pcco.order_time
FROM pizza_clean_customer_orders pcco
LEFT JOIN pizza_names pn ON pn.pizza_id = pcco.pizza_id

params.description: Provides one row per pizza order line with customer and pizza descriptive fields (order-level id, customer id, pizza id and name, plus exclusions, extras, and order time).
params.when_to_use: Retrieve detailed order lines for analytics or reporting that need pizza identity and customer linkage (e.g., list orders with pizza names and customizations). | Compose aggregations at the order-line grain (e.g., counts of pizza lines, counts by pizza_name, time-series of pizza lines). | Join to dimensional attributes keyed by customer_id, pizza_id, or order_time (date) when those joins are one-to-one or many-to-one into this view's grain.
params.output_schema: order_id: unique identifier for the order line at the view grain — derives from pizza_clean_customer_orders.order_id | customer_id: identifier of the customer who placed the order — derives from pizza_clean_customer_orders.customer_id | pizza_id: identifier of the pizza/product on this order line — derives from pizza_clean_customer_orders.pizza_id | pizza_name: human-readable pizza name for the pizza_id — derives from pizza_names.pizza_name (via LEFT JOIN on pizza_id) | exclusions: list or representation of toppings/exclusions applied to this pizza line — derives from pizza_clean_customer_orders.exclusions | extras: list or representation of extra toppings/items applied to this pizza line — derives from pizza_clean_customer_orders.extras | order_time: timestamp (or datetime) when the order was placed — derives from pizza_clean_customer_orders.order_time
params.grounded_columns: pizza_clean_customer_orders.order_id | pizza_clean_customer_orders.customer_id | pizza_clean_customer_orders.pizza_id | pizza_clean_customer_orders.exclusions | pizza_clean_customer_orders.extras | pizza_clean_customer_orders.order_time | pizza_names.pizza_id | pizza_names.pizza_name
params.metric: There are no aggregate measures computed in this view; all output columns are row-level attributes copied or joined from base tables. | If you derive metrics from this view, define them at the view grain (one row = one order line). Example safe derived metrics to compute on top of this view: | order_lines_count = COUNT(*)  -- counts order lines (one per row in this view) | distinct_orders_count = COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)  -- counts unique orders across order lines | unique_customers = COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)  -- unique customers in the selected rows
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to pizza_names ON pizza_id — safe because pizza_names.pizza_id is expected to be one row per pizza_id (the view already left-joined that table and presents pizza_name as a 1:1 attribute). Joining other dimension tables that are 1:1 or many-to-one by pizza_id, customer_id, or by a derived order_date (from order_time) is safe and will not duplicate measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to companies_with_industry_and_dates ON customer_id = company_id (only if customer_id maps one-to-one to company_id) — safe when the target is truly a 1:1 enrichment table. Verify target view/table has one row per company/company_id before joining. | DO NOT join directly to one-to-many tables/views (without aggregation) such as pizza_recipe_topping_expansion, pizza_toppings_with_names, clean_runner_orders_numeric (if it expands lines), or any reshaped/expanded tables that produce multiple rows per pizza_id or order_id. Example: pizza_recipe_topping_expansion likely expands a pizza recipe into multiple topping rows; joining it directly on pizza_id or order_id will multiply this view's rows and thus duplicate counts/metrics. | If you need attributes from a one-to-many source, first aggregate that source to the order-line grain (order_id or pizza_id) before joining. For instance, to attach a 'topping_count' metric from pizza_recipe_topping_expansion, compute topping_count_by_pizza = SELECT pizza_id, COUNT(*) AS topping_count FROM pizza_recipe_topping_expansion GROUP BY pizza_id, then join topping_count_by_pizza ON pizza_id — this preserves cardinality. | When composing time-series or aggregates by order_time (date), you may join to date-dimension tables (one row per date) on DATE(order_time) — safe because date dimension is many-to-one relative to this view (each order_time maps to one date row). | When joining to sibling analytic aggregates (e.g., orders_with_runner_metrics, company_funding_summary_by_company, latest_statistics_per_state), confirm the sibling view's grain: if the sibling is aggregated to order_id or customer_id (one row per order or per customer) the join is safe on that key; if the sibling is at a coarser grain (e.g., company-level or state-level), joining directly will duplicate rows and you must aggregate this view first to that coarser grain (e.g., GROUP BY company_id or state) before joining.

views.description: Denormalized cleaned customer orders joined to pizza name. One row per cleaned order. Useful for order-level reporting with pizza descriptive attributes. | Use for: Order counts by pizza_name over time; Customer-level purchase history; Filter orders by presence of extras/exclusions

views.name: pizza_recipe_topping_expansion
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  pizza_id,
  CAST(trim(value) AS INTEGER) AS topping_id
FROM (
  SELECT
    pizza_id,
    -- split by comma into rows using recursive CTE pattern emulation via json_each workaround
    -- wrap toppings as JSON array by replacing commas with '","' and surrounding with [""]
    -- then use json_each to unnest. If toppings is NULL or empty, no rows produced.
    replace(replace('[' || '"' || replace(toppings, ',', '","') || '"' || ']', '""', '"') , '[""]', '[]') AS toppings_json
  FROM pizza_recipes
) pr, json_each(pr.toppings_json)
WHERE value <> ''

params.description: Exploded (one-row-per) mapping of pizza recipes to individual topping IDs by parsing the comma-separated toppings string.
params.when_to_use: List all topping IDs for each pizza when you need one row per (pizza_id, topping_id). | Filter, join, or aggregate toppings by topping_id across pizzas (e.g., count pizzas that include a given topping). | Compose into joins with topping metadata or orders to attribute pizzas to toppings without re-parsing the original comma list.
params.output_schema: pizza_id: identifier of the pizza recipe — comes from pizza_recipes.pizza_id in the base table. | topping_id: integer ID of a single topping parsed from the pizza_recipes.toppings text field — derived from the parsed json_each value and cast to INTEGER (source: pizza_recipes.toppings via the intermediate toppings_json and json_each(value)).
params.metric: topping_id = CAST(trim(value) AS INTEGER)  -- value is each element produced by json_each over the constructed toppings_json (which is derived from pizza_recipes.toppings)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a toppings dimension (e.g., pizza_toppings_with_names) on topping_id — safe because this view has exactly one row per (pizza_id, topping_id), so joining on topping_id to a one-row-per-topping dimension will not duplicate rows or measures. | Safe to join to a pizzas/pizza_recipes dimension on pizza_id (for example to bring in pizza metadata) — safe because that dimension is expected to be one-row-per-pizza, so it will not multiply this view's rows. | Do NOT join this view directly to any one-to-many table (e.g., an orders table with multiple order lines per pizza or a table with multiple records per (pizza_id, topping_id)) without careful re-aggregation, because such joins will multiply rows and thus duplicate counts/measures derived from this view. If you need to combine with a one-to-many table, either: |   - aggregate the one-to-many table up to pizza_id (or topping_id) before joining, or |   - perform the join and then re-aggregate (for example, COUNT(DISTINCT pizza_id) if you want unique pizzas), | When composing aggregates: treat this view as the canonical set of (pizza_id, topping_id) pairs. For example, to get number of pizzas per topping: SELECT topping_id, COUNT(DISTINCT pizza_id) FROM pizza_recipe_topping_expansion GROUP BY topping_id — COUNT(DISTINCT pizza_id) is safe if you have later joined to tables that could duplicate pizza rows.

views.description: Explodes pizza_recipes.toppings delimited list into one row per (pizza_id, topping_id) for joining to pizza_toppings. Useful when analyzing topping popularity per pizza. Assumes toppings are comma-separated integers in the toppings text. | Use for: Count how often each topping appears across pizzas; Join to pizza_toppings to get topping_name per pizza; Find pizzas containing a particular topping_id

views.name: pizza_toppings_with_names
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  topping_id,
  topping_name
FROM pizza_toppings
views.description: Simple pass-through of toppings lookup. Use when queries need topping_name by topping_id. | Use for: Lookup topping_name for display or joins; Aggregate topping usage with readable names

views.name: orders_with_runner_metrics
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  o.order_id,
  o.customer_id,
  o.pizza_id,
  o.order_time,
  r.runner_id,
  r.pickup_time AS runner_pickup_time,
  r.distance AS runner_distance,
  r.duration AS runner_duration,
  r.cancellation AS runner_cancellation
FROM pizza_clean_customer_orders o
LEFT JOIN clean_runner_orders_numeric r ON r.order_id = o.order_id

params.description: Per-order rows that attach runner assignment and numeric runner metrics (pickup time, distance, duration, cancellation) to each customer pizza order.
params.when_to_use: Get runner-related details for a specific order or a set of orders (e.g., what runner handled order_id X and what were their pickup_time/distance/duration). | Filter or aggregate orders by runner attributes (e.g., average runner_distance per runner or per time window) when starting from one row per order. | Compose higher-level metrics about order fulfillment times or runner performance by aggregating the per-order runner metrics. | Join order-level runner metrics to order-level dimensions (customer, pizza) without duplicating measures.
params.output_schema: order_id: Unique identifier of the order — derived from pizza_clean_customer_orders.order_id (base table alias o). Grain: one row per order_id. | customer_id: Identifier of the customer who placed the order — derived from pizza_clean_customer_orders.customer_id (o.customer_id). | pizza_id: Identifier of the pizza ordered — derived from pizza_clean_customer_orders.pizza_id (o.pizza_id). | order_time: Timestamp when the customer placed the order — derived from pizza_clean_customer_orders.order_time (o.order_time). | runner_id: Identifier of the runner assigned to the order (nullable) — derived from clean_runner_orders_numeric.runner_id (r.runner_id) via LEFT JOIN on order_id. | runner_pickup_time: Runner pickup timestamp for this order (nullable) — derived from clean_runner_orders_numeric.pickup_time (r.pickup_time) and exposed as runner_pickup_time. | runner_distance: Numeric distance metric recorded for the runner on this order (nullable) — derived from clean_runner_orders_numeric.distance (r.distance). | runner_duration: Numeric duration metric recorded for the runner on this order (nullable) — derived from clean_runner_orders_numeric.duration (r.duration). | runner_cancellation: Cancellation flag/indicator recorded for the runner/order (nullable) — derived from clean_runner_orders_numeric.cancellation (r.cancellation).
params.grounded_columns: pizza_clean_customer_orders.order_id | pizza_clean_customer_orders.customer_id | pizza_clean_customer_orders.pizza_id | pizza_clean_customer_orders.order_time | clean_runner_orders_numeric.order_id | clean_runner_orders_numeric.runner_id | clean_runner_orders_numeric.pickup_time | clean_runner_orders_numeric.distance | clean_runner_orders_numeric.duration | clean_runner_orders_numeric.cancellation
params.metric: runner_pickup_time = direct column copy from clean_runner_orders_numeric.pickup_time (no aggregation) | runner_distance = direct numeric metric from clean_runner_orders_numeric.distance (no aggregation) | runner_duration = direct numeric metric from clean_runner_orders_numeric.duration (no aggregation) | runner_cancellation = direct flag/indicator from clean_runner_orders_numeric.cancellation (no aggregation)
params.composition: Join to order-level dimensions/views on pizza_clean_customer_orders.order_id (e.g., orders_with_pizza_and_customer_clean) — safe because this view has exactly one row per order_id (LEFT JOIN preserves one row per order), so joining on order_id to another one-row-per-order view will not duplicate measures. | Join to customer dimension on customer_id (e.g., customer dimension table keyed by customer_id) — safe because this view is one-row-per-order; joining to a one-row-per-customer dimension will not duplicate order-level measures. | Join to pizza dimension on pizza_id (e.g., pizza recipe or pizza metadata keyed by pizza_id) — safe because pizza_id is many-to-one from orders to pizza; joining to a single-row-per-pizza dimension will not duplicate order rows or measures. | Do NOT directly join this view to any view/table that is one-to-many from order_id (e.g., a runner event log with multiple events per order) without first aggregating that other table to one row per order_id. Such a direct join would multiply this view's rows and therefore multiply its per-order measures (runner_distance, runner_duration, etc.). | Do NOT join to pizza_recipe_topping_expansion or pizza_toppings_with_names directly on order_id if those are one-to-many per pizza/order; instead, aggregate toppings (e.g., COUNT, ARRAY_AGG) by order_id first, or join to a pizza-level dimension (one-row-per-pizza) to avoid duplicating order rows. | When computing higher-level metrics (e.g., average runner_distance per runner_id), group/aggregate explicitly: SELECT runner_id, AVG(runner_distance) FROM orders_with_runner_metrics WHERE runner_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY runner_id. This prevents accidental row multiplication. | If joining to clean_runner_orders_numeric for additional runner-level details, prefer joining on runner_id to a runner dimension keyed by runner_id (one-row-per-runner) — safe because orders_with_runner_metrics is one-row-per-order and such a join will not change the cardinality of orders. Avoid joining back to clean_runner_orders_numeric on order_id (the source of this view) unless you intend to reintroduce the original row-level relationship.

views.description: One row per order enriched with runner numeric metrics when available (distance/duration) by left-joining the normalized runner orders. Useful for combining order-level info with delivery performance. | Use for: Assess delivery time vs order time; Compute average delivery duration per pizza or customer; Identify cancelled deliveries

views.name: company_funding_summary_by_company
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  company_id,
  MAX(valuation) AS valuation,
  MAX(funding) AS funding
FROM companies_funding
GROUP BY company_id

params.description: Per-company summary of the maximum reported valuation and funding recorded in companies_funding.
params.when_to_use: Answering questions about each company's highest reported valuation and highest reported funding amount. | Joining per-company financial summary onto a company dimension to build dashboards showing valuation/funding by industry, date ranges, or other company attributes (keeping one row per company). | Using as a building block for further aggregation (e.g., total valuation or funding by industry) by re-aggregating these per-company measures.
params.output_schema: company_id: unique identifier for the company — derived from companies_funding.company_id (GROUP BY key). | valuation: the maximum valuation observed for the company — derived from MAX(companies_funding.valuation). | funding: the maximum funding observed for the company — derived from MAX(companies_funding.funding).
params.metric: valuation = MAX(companies_funding.valuation)  -- per company_id | funding = MAX(companies_funding.funding)      -- per company_id
params.composition: Safe: join to a company dimension or lookup that is one-row-per-company (for example companies_with_industry_and_dates) on company_id — safe because this view has exactly one row per company_id, so joining to a one-to-one company dimension will not duplicate measures. | Safe: aggregate these measures after joining to a dimension (e.g., SUM(valuation) BY industry) — this is correct because you are re-aggregating the one-row-per-company measures at the desired grain. | Not safe without re-aggregation: do NOT join directly to any one-to-many detail table or view (for example orders_with_pizza_and_customer_clean, pizza_recipe_topping_expansion, pizza_toppings_with_names, clean_runner_orders_numeric, orders_with_runner_metrics, trees_by_ntaname, income_by_zipcode, latest_statistics_per_state) on company_id if those views/tables have multiple rows per company, because that will multiply the valuation and funding values per company and inflate aggregations. | If you must join to a one-to-many table to filter or enrich rows, do so by either: (a) pre-aggregating the detail to one row per company before joining, or (b) joining in a subquery that selects distinct company_id or uses an EXISTS/IN filter so that the per-company measures from this view remain one row per company. | When composing into higher-level metrics (e.g., total_funding_by_state), always compute SUM(funding) or SUM(valuation) over this view's rows after joining to the appropriate company-level attribute; do not SUM over a join that still contains the one-to-many detail rows.

views.description: Aggregated funding snapshot per company_id exposing total funding and valuation measures. Useful as a stable source of company-level funding metrics. | Use for: Rank companies by valuation or funding; Join company financials to dates or industries

views.name: companies_with_industry_and_dates
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  cd.company_id,
  cd.date_joined,
  cd.year_founded,
  ci.industry
FROM companies_dates cd
LEFT JOIN companies_industries ci ON ci.company_id = cd.company_id

params.description: Provides one-row-per-company join of company dates (join date and year founded) with the company's industry.
params.when_to_use: Report company-level attributes that need company_id, date_joined, year_founded, and industry | Filter companies by industry and then further aggregate by company_id (e.g., count of companies per industry) | Join company-level attributes onto other company-grained facts (funding summaries, orders aggregated to company) while preserving one row per company | Compose with additional company-level enrichments (e.g., latest company statistics or fundraising summaries) when building company-level datasets
params.output_schema: company_id: unique identifier for the company — derived from companies_dates.company_id | date_joined: date the company record indicates the company joined — derived from companies_dates.date_joined | year_founded: year the company was founded — derived from companies_dates.year_founded | industry: industry classification for the company — derived from companies_industries.industry
params.metric: No aggregates/metrics are defined in this view. All output columns are direct columns from base tables (pass-through): company_id = companies_dates.company_id, date_joined = companies_dates.date_joined, year_founded = companies_dates.year_founded, industry = companies_industries.industry
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to company-grained views/tables on company_id — safe because this view has one row per company_id (grain = ['company_id']), so measures from the other side will not be duplicated when the other side is also one-row-per-company. Example: join to company_funding_summary_by_company on company_id — safe because that sibling is an AGG summarized at company level. | Safe to join to latest_statistics_per_state only if you first ensure latest_statistics_per_state is keyed by company_id (it is a state-level RANK view, so do not assume company-level uniqueness). Do NOT join directly unless you aggregate or filter to one-row-per-company. | Do NOT join this view to one-to-many tables/views (e.g., orders tables or any orders_with_* JOIN views that are at the order or runner-order grain) without re-aggregation first, because those will multiply rows per company and thus duplicate company-level attributes if you intend to keep company-level measures. For example, do NOT directly join to orders_with_pizza_and_customer_clean or orders_with_runner_metrics (order-grain) unless you aggregate orders to company_id first (e.g., SUM/COUNT per company) or use a DISTINCT company_id subquery. | When composing aggregations on top of this view (e.g., count companies by industry or average year_founded by industry), aggregate in the outer query; these operations are safe because the view is already at company granularity. | If you need to enrich with pizza or order-level info (sibling JOIN/NORM/RESHAPE views listed), perform the join in a way that prevents row multiplication: either (a) aggregate the order/pizza-side to company_id before joining, or (b) join and then re-aggregate/USE DISTINCT company_id as appropriate.

views.description: Denormalized company descriptor: one row per company_id with founding year, joinable industry. Use for company-level cohorts and time-based analyses. | Use for: Cohort companies by year_founded; Aggregate funding by industry and founding year

views.name: trees_by_ntaname
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  nta_name,
  boroname,
  borocode,
  state,
  COUNT(*) AS tree_count,
  AVG(tree_dbh) AS avg_tree_dbh,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Alive' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS alive_count,
  SUM(CASE WHEN health = 'Good' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS good_health_count
FROM trees
GROUP BY nta_name, boroname, borocode, state

params.description: Aggregated counts and averages of trees by NTA name (neighborhood tabulation area), with borough and state context.
params.when_to_use: Get total tree counts, average trunk diameter (DBH), and simple health/status counts for a specific NTA (nta_name) or a set of NTAs. | Build higher-level geography summaries (e.g., borough-level) by aggregating these NTA-level measures. | Join NTA-level tree metrics to other NTA/demographic datasets for correlation or enrichment (if done cardinality-safely). | Serve dashboards or reports that display neighborhood-level tree inventory and condition statistics.
params.output_schema: nta_name: name/identifier of the Neighborhood Tabulation Area; comes from trees.nta_name (GROUP BY key). | boroname: borough name (contextual attribute); comes from trees.boroname (GROUP BY key). | borocode: borough code (contextual attribute); comes from trees.borocode (GROUP BY key). | state: state (contextual attribute); comes from trees.state (GROUP BY key). | tree_count: total number of tree rows in trees for this nta_name (COUNT(*) aggregation over rows in trees). | avg_tree_dbh: average tree trunk diameter (tree_dbh) for this nta_name (AVG(tree_dbh) over trees). | alive_count: count of rows where status = 'Alive' within this nta_name (SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Alive' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)). | good_health_count: count of rows where health = 'Good' within this nta_name (SUM(CASE WHEN health = 'Good' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)).
params.grounded_columns: trees.nta_name | trees.boroname | trees.borocode | trees.state | trees.tree_dbh | trees.status | trees.health
params.metric: tree_count = COUNT(*) over rows grouped by nta_name, boroname, borocode, state | avg_tree_dbh = AVG(tree_dbh) over rows grouped by nta_name, boroname, borocode, state | alive_count = SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'Alive' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) over rows grouped by nta_name, boroname, borocode, state | good_health_count = SUM(CASE WHEN health = 'Good' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) over rows grouped by nta_name, boroname, borocode, state
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a one-row-per-NTA dimension (e.g., an NTA dimension view keyed by nta_name) on nta_name — safe because trees_by_ntaname is one-row-per-nta_name (the GROUP BY keys are nta_name + boroname + borocode + state). Joining on the same key(s) will not duplicate measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a one-row-per-borough dimension on boroname or borocode — safe because borough dimension is one-to-one to the borough fields in this view; measures remain unduplicated when joining by boroname or borocode (ensure you join on the exact same borough identifier used here). | do NOT join without re-aggregation to any one-to-many table keyed to nta_name (for example, a table listing multiple demographic records, events, or addresses per nta_name) because such joins will multiply tree_count, alive_count, good_health_count and distort avg_tree_dbh unless you either (a) aggregate the joined data to one row per nta_name before joining, or (b) join first and then re-aggregate starting from the base tables. | do NOT join to tables that expand by tree-level rows (e.g., other raw trees-like tables or expansions of tree attributes) unless you join on a unique tree identifier and then re-aggregate; joining to another multi-row-per-NTA dataset will require re-aggregation to maintain correct measures. | when composing further aggregations: if you roll up this view to a coarser grain (e.g., borough), compute aggregates from the atomic definitions where possible (sum tree_count, sum alive_count, sum good_health_count, and compute a weighted avg_tree_dbh using SUM(avg_tree_dbh * tree_count) / SUM(tree_count)), or re-run aggregation against the base trees table to avoid precision loss.

views.description: Aggregated tree counts and basic health summary per NTA (neighborhood). One row per nta_name with counts and average dbh. Useful for spatial neighborhood-level tree reporting and joins to income by zipcode. | Use for: Compare tree density across neighborhoods; Relate neighborhood tree health to income or zipcode-level metrics

views.name: income_by_zipcode
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  zipcode,
  Estimate_Total,
  Margin_of_Error_Total,
  Estimate_Median_income,
  Margin_of_Error_Median_income,
  Estimate_Mean_income,
  Margin_of_Error_Mean_income
FROM income_trees

params.description: Provides census-style income summary statistics (total count, median, mean) and their margins of error aggregated at the zipcode level.
params.when_to_use: Get income estimates for a specific zipcode (point-in-time snapshot stored in income_trees). | Map or compare median/mean income across zipcodes. | Compose zipcode-level income statistics with demographic or geographic attributes (as long as joins preserve one-row-per-zipcode). | Use as a building block for larger aggregations (e.g., region-level averages) by re-aggregating its measures appropriately.
params.output_schema: zipcode: ZIP code identifier for the row — sourced from income_trees.zipcode | Estimate_Total: Estimated total population (or total count relevant to the income measure) for the zipcode — sourced from income_trees.Estimate_Total | Margin_of_Error_Total: Margin of error for Estimate_Total — sourced from income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Total | Estimate_Median_income: Estimated median income for the zipcode — sourced from income_trees.Estimate_Median_income | Margin_of_Error_Median_income: Margin of error for Estimate_Median_income — sourced from income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Median_income | Estimate_Mean_income: Estimated mean (average) income for the zipcode — sourced from income_trees.Estimate_Mean_income | Margin_of_Error_Mean_income: Margin of error for Estimate_Mean_income — sourced from income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Mean_income
params.grounded_columns: income_trees.zipcode | income_trees.Estimate_Total | income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Total | income_trees.Estimate_Median_income | income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Median_income | income_trees.Estimate_Mean_income | income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Mean_income
params.metric: Estimate_Total = direct column income_trees.Estimate_Total (no further aggregation in this view) | Margin_of_Error_Total = direct column income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Total | Estimate_Median_income = direct column income_trees.Estimate_Median_income | Margin_of_Error_Median_income = direct column income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Median_income | Estimate_Mean_income = direct column income_trees.Estimate_Mean_income | Margin_of_Error_Mean_income = direct column income_trees.Margin_of_Error_Mean_income
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to zipcode- or zipcode-dimension tables/views (e.g., a zipcode -> city/state lookup) on income_by_zipcode.zipcode = dim_zipcode.zipcode — safe because income_by_zipcode has one row per zipcode, so measures are not duplicated. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to geographic-aggregates that are explicitly one-row-per-zipcode (or that have been pre-aggregated to zipcode) on zipcode — safe because there is a 1:1 relationship between rows. | Do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables/views (for example: orders, customers, addresses, or any view with multiple rows per zipcode such as orders_with_runner_metrics, clean_runner_orders_numeric, orders_with_pizza_and_customer_clean) without re-aggregating the one-to-many side first. Joining them directly will multiply income measures per zipcode and incorrectly inflate totals/averages. | If you need to combine with a one-to-many relation (e.g., orders or companies) to compute region-level income-weighted metrics or totals, first aggregate the one-to-many table to one row per zipcode (e.g., SUM, COUNT per zipcode) and then join; alternatively, perform the join and then re-aggregate grouping by zipcode (or by the desired higher-level key) to avoid duplication. | When computing derived metrics across multiple zipcodes (e.g., regional average median income), re-aggregate the Estimate_Median_income and Estimate_Mean_income using appropriate weighting (for mean: weight by counts/population if available; for median: medians cannot be averaged directly without microdata — prefer re-computing from base data or treat as descriptive for each zipcode). | This view is suitable as a stable, one-row-per-zipcode building block. It does not contain row-level microdata, so any composition that requires microdata-level statistical combines (accurate pooled medians or margins of error) must return to the underlying source (income_trees) or use appropriate statistical pooling formulas.

views.description: Pass-through of income estimates per zipcode with preserved original column names. Use when joining socioeconomic data to spatial features like trees. | Use for: Join income to trees by zipcode; Analyze median income vs tree_count

views.name: latest_statistics_per_state
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  date,
  state,
  total_cases,
  total_deaths,
  RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY date DESC) AS date_rank
FROM statistics

params.description: For each state and date, returns the raw totals (cases and deaths) plus a per-state descending date rank (1 = most recent date for that state).
params.when_to_use: Find the latest (most recent) statistics per state by filtering where date_rank = 1. | Compare trends across dates within a single state using the per-state date_rank ordering. | Compose into further queries that need a stable one-row-per-(state,date) atomic fact with a per-state rank to pick or window over recent rows.
params.output_schema: date: reporting date for the statistics — derived directly from statistics.date | state: state identifier (e.g., abbreviation or name depending on source) — derived directly from statistics.state | total_cases: cumulative or total case count reported on that date for that state — derived directly from statistics.total_cases | total_deaths: cumulative or total death count reported on that date for that state — derived directly from statistics.total_deaths | date_rank: integer rank produced by RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY state ORDER BY date DESC); 1 indicates the most recent date for that state
params.metric: date_rank = RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY statistics.state ORDER BY statistics.date DESC) | total_cases = statistics.total_cases (passthrough column, no aggregation in this view) | total_deaths = statistics.total_deaths (passthrough column, no aggregation in this view)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to a state-level dimension (e.g., a states or regions table keyed by state) on latest_statistics_per_state.state = states.state_key — safe because latest_statistics_per_state is at the grain (state, date) and joining to a one-row-per-state dimension does not multiply rows or measures. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to other one-row-per-(state,date) views/tables on (state, date) — safe because keys match the view's grain so measures are not duplicated. | do NOT join directly to any table or view that is one-to-many from state (for example, a per-county or per-day-events table keyed to state) without first aggregating that table to the (state) or (state,date) grain. Such joins would multiply rows and incorrectly inflate totals (total_cases, total_deaths) because latest_statistics_per_state contains one row per (state,date) and is not pre-aggregated over the many-side. | do NOT join to sibling views that expand rows (RESHAPE or JOIN that produce multiple rows per state like pizza_recipe_topping_expansion or orders_with_pizza_and_customer_clean) without aggregating the sibling to the matching (state) or (state,date) grain first. If you need sums or averages of the expanded data alongside these measures, aggregate the expanded data to (state) or (state,date) and then join. | When composing metrics (for example, computing per-capita rates using a population dimension), prefer joining the one-row-per-state population table on state to compute derived metrics; this preserves cardinality and ensures total_cases and total_deaths remain correct.

views.description: Latest statistics row per state based on date. Exposes a state-level latest flag and rank for selecting most recent snapshot per state. | Use for: Select the latest statistics per state (WHERE date_rank = 1); Trend analyses using per-state time series

views.name: trees_with_income_by_zip
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  trees.idx,
  trees.tree_id,
  trees.spc_common,
  trees.address,
  trees.zipcode,
  trees.boroname,
  income_trees.Estimate_Median_income,
  income_trees.Estimate_Mean_income
FROM trees
JOIN income_trees
  ON trees.zipcode = income_trees.zipcode
WHERE trees.zipcode IS NOT NULL
  AND income_trees.zipcode IS NOT NULL

semantic_filters.Ensure_matched_income: income_trees.zipcode IS NOT NULL AND trees.zipcode IS NOT NULL

views.description: Denormalized row-level relation that joins trees to income information by zipcode so each tree row carries the matched income estimates. Matches on zipcode; intended to supply one row per tree with associated income census fields when a matching income row exists.

views.name: trees_canonicalized_location
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  idx,
  tree_id,
  spc_common,
  TRIM(address) AS address,
  CASE
    WHEN zipcode = '' THEN NULL
    ELSE zipcode
  END * 1 AS zipcode,
  LOWER(TRIM(boroname)) AS boroname_norm
FROM trees
WHERE idx IS NOT NULL
grain: one row per idx (one row per tree)
views.description: Cleans and canonicalizes tree location and borough fields. Produces trimmed/normalized boroname and zipcode as numeric, and exposes key tree identifiers. Useful for grouping and joining to external geography/income tables.

views.name: income_by_zip_filtered_positive
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  zipcode,
  Estimate_Median_income,
  Estimate_Mean_income
FROM income_trees
WHERE Estimate_Median_income > 0
  AND Estimate_Mean_income > 0
grain: zipcode (one row per income zipcode record)
views.description: Subset of income_trees restricted to rows with positive median and mean income estimates. Keeps zipcode and raw income measures for joins and aggregations.

views.name: trees_by_boroname_health
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  tree_id,
  boroname,
  zipcode,
  borocode,
  health,
  status,
  spc_common,
  spc_latin,
  latitude,
  longitude,
  address
FROM trees
views.description: Row-level cohort of trees exposing location and health attributes to allow filtering and aggregation by borough name and health status.

views.name: trees_location_summary
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  boroname,
  health,
  status,
  COUNT(tree_id) AS count_trees
FROM trees
GROUP BY
  boroname,
  health,
  status
views.description: Aggregated counts of trees by borough name and health and status to support percentage and distribution queries per borough.

views.name: trees_basic_geography
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  tree_id AS tree_id,
  address AS address,
  boroname AS boroname,
  borocode AS boro_code,
  zipcode AS zipcode,
  latitude AS latitude,
  longitude AS longitude
FROM trees
views.description: Canonicalized tree-level projection with cleaned geographic and id columns (ensures consistent column names and exposes keys and location for joins and filters).

views.name: companies_with_dates_and_funding
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  cf.company_id,
  cf.valuation,
  cd.date_joined
FROM companies_funding AS cf
LEFT JOIN companies_dates AS cd
  ON cf.company_id = cd.company_id
views.description: Denormalized company-level rows combining funding/valuation with company date metadata. One row per company_id exposing valuation and the raw date_joined for year extraction and filtering.

views.name: company_industries
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  company_id,
  industry
FROM
  companies_industries
WHERE
  company_id IS NOT NULL
  AND industry IS NOT NULL
grain: company_id, industry  -- one row per company-industry association
views.description: Mapping of companies to industries. One row per company_id and industry. Keeps company_id and industry for joins and counts; allows counting a company multiple times if it is in multiple industries.

views.name: unicorns_by_company_year_industry
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  ci.industry AS industry,
  CAST(STRFTIME('%Y', cjd.date_joined) AS INTEGER) AS year,
  COUNT(DISTINCT ci.company_id) AS unicorn_company_count
FROM
  companies_with_industry_and_dates cjd
  JOIN company_industries ci USING (company_id)
GROUP BY
  ci.industry,
  CAST(STRFTIME('%Y', cjd.date_joined) AS INTEGER)
grain: industry, year  -- one row per industry per year
views.description: Pre-aggregated counts of unicorn companies per industry per year. Counts a company for each industry it belongs to. Year is extracted from companies_dates.date_joined. This view is a helpful intermediate for yearly industry-level metrics.

views.name: pizza_order_items_normalized
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  pco.order_id AS order_id,
  pco.customer_id AS customer_id,
  pco.pizza_id AS pizza_id,
  -- canonicalize timestamp: keep as stored text but normalize common ISO-like formats by trimming whitespace
  TRIM(pco.order_time) AS order_time,
  TRIM(pco.extras) AS extras,
  TRIM(pco.exclusions) AS exclusions
FROM pizza_clean_customer_orders pco
views.description: Normalized order-line level rows for each pizza order linking order, pizza, and textual extras/exclusions so ingredients can be counted. Cleans IDs and canonicalizes timestamps. One row per order_id x pizza_id with raw extras/exclusions text preserved for further parsing or joins.

views.name: pizza_recipe_topping_pairs
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  pizza_recipes.pizza_id AS pizza_id,
  CAST(trim(t.value) AS INTEGER) AS topping_id
FROM pizza_recipes,
  -- split comma-separated toppings into rows using recursive CTE pattern emulation via sqlite's json functions:
  -- transform string into JSON array then use json_each to iterate
  json_each(
    -- wrap toppings in brackets to form a valid JSON array; handle NULL/empty by replacing with '[]'
    CASE
      WHEN pizza_recipes.toppings IS NULL OR trim(pizza_recipes.toppings) = '' THEN '[]'
      ELSE '[' || pizza_recipes.toppings || ']'
    END
  ) AS t
views.description: Exploded mapping of pizza_id to individual topping_id values derived from the recipes table's comma-separated toppings field. One row per pizza_id x topping_id (topping_id as integer); suitable for joining to topping names and aggregating ingredient usage.

views.name: topping_master
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  topping_id,
  topping_name
FROM pizza_toppings
views.description: Canonical topping master list mapping topping_id to topping_name for human-readable ingredient names.

views.name: pizza_order_cohort
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  o.order_id AS order_id,
  o.customer_id AS customer_id,
  o.pizza_id AS pizza_id,
  o.order_time AS order_time,
  o.extras AS extras_raw,
  o.exclusions AS exclusions_raw,
  r.runner_id AS runner_id,
  r.runner_pickup_time AS runner_pickup_time,
  r.runner_cancellation AS runner_cancellation_raw
FROM orders_with_pizza_and_customer_clean o
LEFT JOIN orders_with_runner_metrics r
  ON o.order_id = r.order_id
views.description: One-row-per-customer-order cohort with key identifiers and raw referenced fields from customer and runner tables to allow filtering by pizza type and cancellation status.

views.name: pizza_extras_counts
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  o.order_id AS order_id,
  COALESCE(pe.extras_count,
           CASE
             WHEN trim(o.extras) = '' OR o.extras IS NULL THEN 0
             ELSE (
               -- count commas and add 1, but handle single-item with no commas
               LENGTH(o.extras) - LENGTH(REPLACE(o.extras, ',', '')) + 1
             )
           END
          ) AS extras_count,
  CASE WHEN pe.extras_count IS NOT NULL THEN 'normalized_table'
       WHEN trim(o.extras) IS NULL OR trim(o.extras) = '' THEN 'parsed_text_empty'
       ELSE 'parsed_text_counted'
  END AS extras_count_source
FROM
  pizza_customer_orders o
LEFT JOIN
  pizza_get_extras pe
ON
  o.order_id = pe.order_id
grain: order_id (one row per order with a canonical extras_count)
views.description: Number of extras per order, preferring explicit extras_count from normalized extras table, and falling back to counting comma-separated items in raw extras text. Exposes a canonical extras_count per order and a flag indicating source of the count.

views.name: pizza_menu_ids
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  pizza_id,
  pizza_name
FROM pizza_names
views.description: Canonical mapping of pizza identifiers to their names; exposes pizza_id and pizza_name to allow exact-match filtering on pizza names.

views.name: word_list_filtered_by_length_and_prefix
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  words AS word,
  length(words) AS length
FROM
  word_list
WHERE
  length(words) BETWEEN 4 AND 5
  AND (substr(words,1,1) = 'r' OR 1=1)
views.description: Subset of word_list restricted to words with a canonical length and optional prefix; useful for queries that operate on words of particular lengths and starting characters.

views.name: word_list_canonical_signature
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  words AS word,
  LENGTH(words) AS length,
  (SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(ch, '') FROM (
      SELECT SUBSTR(words, i, 1) AS ch
      FROM (
        SELECT 1 AS i UNION ALL SELECT 2 UNION ALL SELECT 3 UNION ALL SELECT 4 UNION ALL SELECT 5
        UNION ALL SELECT 6 UNION ALL SELECT 7 UNION ALL SELECT 8 UNION ALL SELECT 9 UNION ALL SELECT 10
        UNION ALL SELECT 11 UNION ALL SELECT 12 UNION ALL SELECT 13 UNION ALL SELECT 14 UNION ALL SELECT 15
        UNION ALL SELECT 16 UNION ALL SELECT 17 UNION ALL SELECT 18 UNION ALL SELECT 19 UNION ALL SELECT 20
        UNION ALL SELECT 21 UNION ALL SELECT 22 UNION ALL SELECT 23 UNION ALL SELECT 24 UNION ALL SELECT 25
        UNION ALL SELECT 26 UNION ALL SELECT 27 UNION ALL SELECT 28 UNION ALL SELECT 29 UNION ALL SELECT 30
        UNION ALL SELECT 31 UNION ALL SELECT 32 UNION ALL SELECT 33 UNION ALL SELECT 34 UNION ALL SELECT 35
        UNION ALL SELECT 36 UNION ALL SELECT 37 UNION ALL SELECT 38 UNION ALL SELECT 39 UNION ALL SELECT 40
      ) positions
      WHERE i <= LENGTH(words)
      ORDER BY ch
  )) AS signature
FROM word_list
views.description: Normalized representation of each word with its length and a canonical anagram signature (sorted characters, case-sensitive). Useful to identify anagram groups and perform joins/grouping by signature.
